GOVERNOR EYRE AND THE BRITISH
PARLIAMENT.

THE House of Commons on Monday last
voted 4t,123 to defray the legal expenses in-
-caned during his trial by ex-Governor EYRE.
.Two hundred and forty-three English gentle-
men interested in the honour and reputation
-of the country—Christian men—men engaged
in the daily practice of ordinary fashionable
philanthropies, have thus given their sanction
,to a piece of human butcherwork as shocking
as any recorded on the darkest page of human
history.

Against Mr. EYRE himself, no Englishman
can be presumed to entertain any feeling of per-
sonal hostility. Judged in himself, upon his own
merits, before he became Governor of Jamaica,
he seems to have been a man possessing many
amiable qualities—a man with the ability to
make friends and to retain permanently their
esteem. With this, however, the nation has
little to do. It is as Governor of Jamaica the
people of England have to do with him,
because it was in this capacity he performed the
deeds which have brought his name promi-
nently and painfully into question, and because
these deeds must seriously affect the reputa-
tion of England—must, if we condone them
or approve of them, stamp us with an
ineffaceable infamy in the eyes of all just,
.law-abiding, humane people. The four thou-
sand and odd pounds are nothing—were they
forty thousaml they would not be Worth a
thought compared with the implied sanction
they 'carry of wanton, lawless, brutal slaughter
committed on helpless people in a blindness of
rage which obliterated all power of discrimina-
tion,whioh struck alike at the innocent and the
guilty, and which, by its savage disregard of
justice, brought the .principle of authority
into contempt, and made Government, for the
moment, as hateful as the most blind and
ferocious anarchy.'

to recite here the events as they followed

close of that shocking Jamaica saturnalia.

THE PEOPLE'S PAPER.

These Jamaica revolters belonged to a
degraded, servile race; to a race of workers
who suffered from grievous wrongs, or at least
imagined they did. To suppress rebellion and
do justice was not the first thought in the mind
of EYRE, nor is it the paramount thought with
our parliamentary classes. To kill without
mercy, to teach by terrible example, is their
prevailing idea. To murder those who load,
or are supposed to lead, and to crush by blood-
letting and torture in as shocking a manner as
possible those who follow such leaders has
always been the plan and purpose of men
whose business it is to govern, and whose fit-
ness for governing lies in a belief in the reck-
lessness of force rather than in a possession of
wisdom or a love of justice. Under such cir-
cumstances how could it be expected th 4 the
British Parliament could be anything but
friendly to Governor EYRE. There is, perhaps,
too much blood on his hands to set him up again
as a Governor of any other British possession;
but a condonation is of value, monermay con-
sole, and the British people, much as they hate
the whole business, with such a Parliament as
they have got have nothing for it but to
submit to the payment of this detestable
blood-money.

Mr, clwisTosE's plea of an engagement by
the last Government was worthy a pettifogger
with a bad case; but it was utterly inadmis-
sible in the mouth of wstatesman, and from
.Mr. GLADSTONE as First Minister of the Crown,
in the present state of the public mind, it was
absolute folly. The past Government asked
for Mr. EYRE'S bill, and because they did so,
the present Government consider themselves
bound to pay it. There can be no engage-
ment here, either moral or legal, and as the
reputation of England was bound up in the
transaction, they were bound to show that they
in no way sanctioned the Jamaica atrocities,
and if her MAJESTY'S Ministers were as anzious
to hold the nation bound to the claims of
justice and humanity, as they were to hold
themselves bound by the acts of their pre-
decessors, so nefarious a transaction as that
of Monday night could not have taken place.
Of course Mr. GLADSTONE knew he was safe
with a Tory support. He knew that the country
gentlemen would go with him, even. though
the Jamaica massacres, manglings, and
burnings were, if possible, of a much
more atrocious character. How do they know
but that the present discontent of the agri-
cultural labourers may be provoked into riot,
and, if such unhappily should be the ease, it
would never do if those in authority were so
discouraged as to be squeamish about killing,
If they want a terrible example, as possibly
they may, reeldessness as to human life will
be necessary, and such a contingency must be
prepared for.

The whole affair in its spirit is simply
detestable. All the offences Mr. GIADSTONE
and his Government have given to the
Liberal English people do not amount to half
the sum of this single act. And it is no ex-
aggeration to say that the position of the
Liberal administration has been infinitely
injured by this act of supreme folly. The
Conservatives in supporting him did their
proper and natural work, and when the general
election comes they will add profit to what is
.now a pleasure. It is true a support given to
Tories by Liberal electors would be, even for
this reason, an inconsistent ththg, but whfu
people- are provoked and disgusted„ logic bus
little to do with the regulation of their ac-

running together in the House of Commons,
and confounding themselves by indiscriminate
votes, it need not be wondered at if the people
outside lose the power of distinguishing be-
tween them, and try to find different principles
and also different leaders to those by whom
they are now,led, sometimes in one direction
and sometimes in another, and not unfre-
quently into the filthiest bye-paths of party
convenience. It may truly be said that, as
far as the Liberal party is concerned, the vote
of Monday evening last was a great cala-

his duty to defend it to the last extremity.
Few would have blamed him or thought of
blaming him for any severe measure he might
have resorted to for the purpose of bolding
the rights of the British crown intact.
If, through cowardice or imprudence, he had
allowed the authority entrusted to his keeping
to drop from his hands, he would have been
despised and punished on his return to his
native land, because all necessary power was
placed at his disposal for the vindication and
maintenance of his authority as Governor of
the Island. But surely one of the first
conditions of power is that it shall not be
abused; that that which is meant as a pro-
tection shall not be turned into an oppression ;
that that which in its right exercise is a
blessing shall not be allowed to transform
itself into a curse.

Now, it may be asked in all fairness, if it
was in this spirit Governor EYRE and those
under him uphold the power and the rights of
the British Crown? Was there a line of any
kind drawn between the rebellion, if it could
at any time be so called—existent, and the re-
bellion hopelessly crushed and trodden out?
Hero is Mr. Bo witrNo's description of what
took place drawn from the report of the Royal
Commission. "Up to the 20th of October
-Governor Ernu was justified in all the steps
he took; but for thirty days, from the date of
the proclamation of martial law, homesteads
were destroyed, villages were burnt, ' and
people were sacrificed without regard to age
or sex. Governor EyrtE stated that the houses
burnt were only negro huts, but these villages
had been compared to the villages of Switzer-
land for beauty, and the inhabitants were
described as living in comfort, and in some
cases in downright luxury The total number
of persons put to death during the existence of
martial law was 439, of. whom 351 were con-
demned by courts-martial, fifty were shot or
hung without trial, twenty-five wore shot by
the Maroons, and ten otherwise killed. Of the
whole number 114 were put to death before
the 20th of October, fifty-two on that
day, and 273 wore executed in the twenty-
five days following. The total number of
-persons flogged was six hundred, and as many
as 100 lashes were given to one man and
thirty to a woman. One man, after being
tried and receiving fifty lashes, was tried a
second time and executed, and another was
tried three times and at last executed."—But
why further allude to this devil's rigadoon ?
this grotesque dance of devastation and death,
in which arson was a jest and murder an
amusement? The British . people have been
shocked and sickened by it from the first
moment its awful details wore made known.
How the working men of England regard it
there can be no doubt, and there is as little
*doubt why the Parliamentary mind and the
Working class mind are at variance, on a ques-
tion so important to the honour and to the
interest of the nation.

Disturbances, emutes, revolts, rebellions,
are usually excited by oppressive laws, or by
unjust and tyrannical methods of administer-
ing the law. Those who engage in them are
usually the poor and down-trodden. The
workers of the world are the usual revolters
against established authority, for they are the
chief sufferers from a tyrannical exercise of
power. On the other hand the law-making
and the law administering classes are those
-whose duty it is to Empress and punish
disturbances, however justly provoked.

THE COMING SOCIAL REVOLUTION.

THE following is the introductory outline to
which a preface was given in the BEE-Hun
of July 6. The final object of the Co-operative
.Social System being to attain the highest
possible happiness of all, by substituting the
causes of good for the causes of evil, in man
and in his surroundings, the truths which are
the basis of the knowledge of these causes
must of course occupy the first place in the
general statement of the subject. The know-
ledge of these truths is the only basis upon
which a character of true enlightenment and
enlightened goodness can be formed. While
we do not know them we are living in in-
tellectual darkness, and in error, in reference
to Subjects of the highest practical importance,
and we must continually experience the deterior-
ating effects of our erroneous ideas; we are living
intellectually and morally, and practically, in
darkness and evil. When we come to under-
stand them we pass intellectually and morally
into the world of light, and of goodness rightly
directed.

TILE LONDON RAILWAY CLEAR-

ING CLERKS.

A general meeting of the clerks of the Railway
Clearing-house was held on Monday evening at
the school-rooms of the Bedford Chapel, Char-
rington-street, Oakley-square, for the purpose of I
considering the expediency of petitioning the com-
mittee for a general revision of the salaries
throughout the office. A very large number of
clerks, amounting to nearly a thousand, assembled,
the chair being taken by Mr. Prioke, who, in his
remarks, spoke in strong terms of the small salaries
now paid to the hundreds of clerks in the employ
of the aloe. He considered it a disgrace to the
managers to expect them to keep body and soul
together on the miserable pittances they were paid.
Railways throughout the kingdom were now in a
most thriving and prosperous condition, and their
revenues were as It rule steadily and daily increasing.
Their directors were surely,therefore, in a position to
afford bettor salaries to the extensive, and to them,
invaluable body of clerks in their common employ.
He proposed as the first resolution :
That a commitee be appointed, consisting of one
representative from each division in each of the de-
partments of the office, to petition for an increase of
twenty per cent. on the salaries now paid to the
clerks.
The proposition having been seconded, and
unanimously carried, the election of the com-
mittee took place in due form.
A speaker, in reforring to the amount of the
increase specified, said that the salaries had
undergone no alteration worth speaking about
since the time when a hundred pounds represented
a far greater value than now, and that, owing to
the great increase of outlay attending the constant
growth in the price of provisions, rent, and
clothing, they were, while demanding the twenty
per cent. additional salary, only seeking pay of
practically the same value as that received twenty
years ago.
A second resolution was also passed to the

effect,
That the committee should not accept any com-
promise with the committee of the clearing-
house without flrat consulting the body of clerks
assembled in a general meeting.
The latter resolution occasioned some sliett
debate end was objected to by some as savouring
somewhat of a strike. The difficulties were, how-
ever, satisfictorily explained away, • and the
proceedings terminated with a cordial vote of
thanks to the chairman.

A. further advance in the price of iron was
reported at the quarterly meeting of the trade
held at Wolverhampton.

Amongst the cases disposed of at tho Old.
Baile,y on Wednesday was a charge, of con-
spiracy against three men named Sheldrake,
-Wallace, and Rowlands, who were indicted for
having endeavoured to fasten an unfounded
accusation of felony against a man named
lloorhouse. Wallace was acquitted, and
Sheldrake and Rowlands were sentenced to
five years' penal servitude and eighteen
mouths respeotively. The trial of James
Daniel Rogers for the murder of his wife was
postponed to next session.

These firms were stated to be Messrs. Wood, Larch
field Foundry, and Messrs. Rhodes' moulding shop.
Mr. Wm. Whitelow (fitter) seconded the resolution,
which was carried.
Mr. Luke Hope moved the next resolution,
which pledged the meeting to support the united
committee until the struggle was carried to a
successful issue. Mr. Todd seconded the pro-
position, which was carried amidst applause.
Mr. David White moved, and Mr. Fowler
(moulder), seconded a resolution pledging those

struggle, it being stated that certain employers
were putting pressure to bear on some of the
prominent movers in it.

vita TItADEB COUNCIL.
The usual monthly meeting of the Leeds and
District Trades Council was held on Wednesday
evening, at Parker's Temperance Hotel; repre-
sentatives front the following trades were pre-
sent :—G. U. carpenters and joiners, clothdressers,
masons, coachmakers, engineers, ironfounders,
millers, tailors, plasterers, cordwainers, hammer-
men, cabinet-makers, and paper-stainers. Mr.
E. C. Denton occupied the chair.
The minutes of the previous meeting having
been confirmed, the Chairman stated that ho had
received communications from Mr. P. Barry,
respecting a now trades newspaper, to be called
Labour, which is to be confined entirely to trade
matters, and wishing the trades of Leeds to
entertain and support it. After some discussion
it was resolved ithat the question should stand
over till the next meeting of the Council.
On the Nino Hours (Factories) Bill, it was
resolved that a petition to the House of Commons
in favour of Mr. Mundella's Bill be prepared and
signed by the officers of the Council, and sent to
Mr. Alderman Carter for presentation.

The Secretary (Mr. Thomas Plackett) then road
over the balance-shoot for the pest year, which
showed 44i income of £7 78. 10d., and an expendi-
ture of £5 18s. 40., leaving a balance of
11 N. .50. to be carried to the next year's
account. It was resolved—That the balance-
sheet be accepted as read, and that 150 copies be
printed and issued to the various trado societies
of Leeds and district.

After completing the revision of the rules, a
conversation ensued on the repot of the Trade .
Union Congress (Parliamentary) Committee. It
was resolved—That the Council approve of the
report issued by the Committee. After a short
discussion on the forthcoming Trades Union Con-
gress to be held in Leeds in January next, the
meeting separated.

HALES OWEN.
TUE STRUM IN TRE NAIL TRADE.

Every day the numbers of common 'milers who
turn out and refuse to work up their iron is largely
increased, and in the districts of Hales Owen, Old
Hill, Rowley, and The Lye, the strike is general.
Some firms in other districts are inclined to concede
to the men the "20 per cent. on the list," and a
few of the masters have already offered the 15 per
cent. This, indeed, has in some instances been
paid. Great dissatisfaction exists amongst the
nailers at the result of the Into meeting of masters,
and that they were not mkt with the same liberal
spirit as the colliers, puddlers, and other work-
men.

articles.title: T AMWOR at. STRIKE or JOINERS.
articles.text:
T AMWOR at.
STRIKE or JOINERS.

The joiners employed by the London and North-
Western Railway Co. at Taraworth, have struck
work for an increme of wages and a reduction in
the hours of labour. About oihte n- weeks ago
the mon made application to the company for a
rise in their Wages of 6d. -per day—namely, from
is, 6d, to as., and - fur the working hours to be

articles.title: MACCLESFIELD. STRIKE OF SILK DYERS.
articles.text:
MACCLESFIELD.
STRIKE OF SILK DYERS.

The Macclesfield silk dyers, to the number of
160, have struck work. About nine months ago
the masters conceded an advance of 2s. per week
and a reduction of the hours of labour to fifty-nine.
The demand now made is that of an advance of
2s. per week and a reduction of the hours of labour
to fifty-four. The masters met on Thursday night,
when it was resolved rather to lock the men out
than concede their demands.

BARNSLEY.
THE WEAVERS.

_
The Barnsley power-loom weavers have issued
a circular asking for an advance of wages on the
ground of the great increase in the price of food,
clothing, coals, and rent, and the prosperity of the
trade. They request an answer at once.

articles.title: BIRMINGHAM.
articles.text:
BIRMINGHAM.

TIIE LOCK-OUT IN LONDON.

A public meeting was held on Thursday even-
ing, at the Public-Office, Moor-street, to take into
consideration the London lock-out and to express
sympathy with the moo. Mr. John Osborne
occupied the chair.
Mr. Broadhurst, mason; Mr. Makin, carpenter;
Mr. Shipton, house painter; Mr. Macnamara,
plasterer; Mr. Baker, smiths and metal workers;
Mr. Mitchell, general union of carpenters, who
formed a deputation from London, explained at
some length the position in which the several
trades were placed.
Mr. J. Price, joiner, moved :—" That this meet-
ing, having hoard the statememt made by the
deputation from London, is of opinion that a
reduction of the hours of labour is necessary to
promote the moral, social, physical, and intel-
lectual well-being and happiness of the people,
and therefore deeply regrets the course taken by
the master builders of London in locking out the
men in their employ, and earnestly hopes that
both parties will endeavour to settle this un-
fortunate dispute by arbitration. In the mean-
time the meeting pledges itself to give them all
the support in its power until the dispute is
brought to a successful issue."
Mr. C. Williams, secretary to the United Asso-
ciation of Plasterers, seconded the resolution,
which was passed amid much applause.
Mr. Crompton moved—" That, in order to give
practical effect to the foregoing resolution, this
meeting requests all societies, factories, shops, and
jobs to send delegates to the weekly meetings,
to be held at the Racket Court Inn, Bath-street,
Birmingham, and that a committee be elected at
this meeting."
Mr. R. Last seconded the proposition, which
was adopted.

articles.title: MIDDLESBROUGH.
articles.text:
MIDDLESBROUGH.

TIIE IRON TRADE AND ARBITRATION.

A largely attended meeting of puddlers and
others connected with the manufactured iron trade
of the north of England was held at the Oxford
Music Hall, Middlesbrough, on Monday, for the
purpose of considering the recent award of 7 per
cent. increase of wages reported to be due by Mr.
Waterhouse, accountant to the Board of Arbitra-
tion and Conciliation. Mr. Kane, the workmen's
secretary at the Board of Arbitration, explained
what was being done in South Staffordshire, and
advised the meeting to wait until the middle of
the month, by which time they would be able to
consider the propriety of asking for a reconsider-
ation of the starting point of the sliding scale.
It was ultimately resolved, "That this meeting
regrets that the information which ought to have
been supplied at an earlier date has partly caused
the men to discontinue work, and having at last
heard the statement, which we accept as satis-
factory, we therefore agree to resume work as
soon as possible, pending the decision of the next
board meeting on the 22nd inst., when the award
in the South Staffordshire trade will be made
known."

articles.title: DISPUTE IN THE LONDON BUILDING TRADES.
articles.text:
THE DISPUTE IN THE LON-
DON BUILDING TRADES.

INTRODUCTION.

With the commencement of the present week
the lock-out assumed a new aspect. This new
aspect is owing to the unexpected action taken by
the masons' committee on Friday last, and en-
dorsed by the men in that branch of the building
trade at a general meeting held on Saturday
evening.
Last Wednesday, it seems, the Society masons,
in a special meeting, empowered a deputation to
seek an interview with the Committee of the
Masters, with full powers to come to terms, if
that were found possible. The interview took
place on Friday, when the deputation succeeded in
its mission, by giving up the principle of the
"movement" for which all the trades in unison
had been supposed to contend—the "nine hours
work at ninepence an hour." Within a fraction
they have secured the terms of time for which
they struck; a new distribution of hours of work
has been made, under which, during twelve weeks
of winter, they will give a shorter time, and the
other forty weeks a longer time—making all the
year round an average of 51f hours. The sub-
stutial compromise, however, has been made on
the question of pay ; the masons and the masters
having agreed to split the difrorence, and fixed
the rate of wages in future at 81d. per hour instead
of 81.
The separate action which the masons have
taken for themselves occasioned a good deal of
excitement among the other trades. In 1859, they
had exhibited such a decided tendency towards
taking care of themseives, that during the present
movement their co-operation was hardly invited or
expected by the other branches of the trades locked
out. From the first they were candid in announcing
that they went on their own footing, and, except-
ing the short conference which was held at the
Brown Bear last Monday afternoon, there has been
no visible community of interest with the parties
who now consider themselves betrayed. A division

in the workmen's camp makes tho settlement of

the dispute really more difficult, instead of less so.
• If the carpenters choose to stand out from the
masons' agreement a great amount of incon-
venience may yet be occasioned. We cannot think
that the masons have acted wisely in this matter,
so far as concerns their obligations to the carpen-
ters. Carpenters and masons must have the same
working hours, and the masons' committee have
either struck a bargain for the carpenters as well

as themselves, or they have done nothing at all.
The carpenters say that in their case the hours
agreed upon by the masons are not suitable.

articles.title: STONEMASONS.
articles.text:
THE STONEMASONS.

On Saturday morning last the building trade
operatives were thrown into a state of consider-
able excitement by learning that on the previous
afternoon a deputation from the masons had
solicited and obtained a private interview with the

committee of the Central Association of Master
Builders, and had arranged terms for the settle-
ment of the dispute so far as their branch of the
trade was concerned.

Mr. Bird, the Masters' Secretary, stated that the
members of the committee of masters had re-
ceived the deputation of masons at their own
request, and the interview had lasted six hours.
lie also stated that ho was not at liberty to give
the resolutions which had been agreed to, but that
he might go so far as to state that such arrange-
ments had been made as would probably end the
dispute. These arrangementi, however, were not
to be made public until they had been submitted
to the general body of masons on Monday.
Shortly before five o'clock on Monday the
general meeting of the masons was held in
Wileoelie's Assembly-rooms, Westminster-bridge-
road, capable of holding abut 703 persons.
The room was crowded. A number of carpenters,
plasterers, and men belonging to other branches
were assembled outside the hall. Peeling was
very high; inside care was taken to exclude all
persons but masons from the meeting; the meeting
was very excited. An interval of silence having
been obtained,

Mr. Skemp was voted to the chair, and stated
that the object of the meeting was to receive and
consider the report of tho deputation who had
the previous day waited upon the employers.

Mr, Broadhurst gave the report, and was
generally cheered. Ile commenced his remarks by
stating that at a special meeting of the Society of
Masons, held on Wednesday evening last, a resolu-
tion was passed empowering the committee to seek
an interview with the committee of masters, with
full powers to arrange, if possible, terms of settle-
ment by which the existing dispute might be
terminated. That intcrview was held on Friday
last, and a settlement had been arrived at, so far,

at least, as the masons were concerned, and it
was in the interests of masons only that the
deputation waited upon the masters. The masons
were the only body of men in tha building trade
thoroughly united in a society, and therefore such
a body ought to have its duo weight and to
exercise an influence over the • building trade.
The employers present at the interview were
Messrs. Hannen, C. Lucas, G. Trollope, G. Dines,
and S. Bird, and the masons who accompanied
him were Wisbett, Bowman, Kennard, and
Weighill. They met the masters' committee at 2
o'clock, and were occupied in discussing all the
points in the case up to 5 o'clock, when, not
seeing any chance of coming to an agreement, the
deputation were about leaving, but one of the
employers suggested another form of arrangement.
This was discussed for another two hours, and
ultimately the following agreement was drawn up
and signed by all present :
Westminster Chambers, July 5.
The Committee of the Central Association of
Master Builders agree to settle the questions now
pending between them and the masons by their
representatives in the following terms :--That
the average working hours shall be 51 hours per
week, as requested by the workmen, but that the
shorter hours during which they cannot see to
work in the winter shall be made up by additional
hours in summer, and that the wages shall be 80.
per hour instead of Bd., as at present. The hours
to be as under-12 weeks in winter at 47 hours
per week, 40 weeks summer at 52i hours. The
hours of commencing to be 6 o'clock in the sum-
mer, 7 o'clock in winter, and 6.30 on Monday
mornings in the summer.. The hour of leaving off
on Saturday to be 12 o'clock all the year round.
The committee of masters will recommend the
members of the association to pay wages on Friday
evening after work.
The deputation, continued Mr. Broadhurst, be-
fore signing this agreement, struggled hard to
obtain the promise of the additional id. per hour
on the Ist of March next, but were unsuccessful.
By the above arrangement the masons would work
12 more hours in the year than 61 per week, and
the wages would be about 6d. per week loss in
summer, and about Bd. per week loss in winter.
He concluded by giving a description of the dis-
cussions between the deputation and the Masters
Committee, and said he was prepared to defend
the agreement which had been made at any time
and in any place. (Cheers.)
Mr. Porter moved,

That the report of the deputAtion be received,
and the agreement signed by the deputation be
endorsed and approved by this meeting.
Mr. Munks seconded the resolution.

Mr. Salter said he was not satisfied with tho-
result of the deputation. This was not the nine
hours for which they had all been struggling,
neither was it the 9d. (gear, hear.) He thought
the masons were strong enough to have had both
if they had waited a little longer. Surely they
were not frightened because they had been locked
out for a few days? If they did not feel them-
selves strong enough to carry out the struggle,
they had no right to have entered into it at all.
He concluded by moving as an amendment :
That this meeting is of opinion our committee
should adhere strictly to the terms of the
memorial-51 hours per week, at 9J. per hour.
A mason in the body of the meeting seconded
the amendment, which, after much noise, was put
to the meeting, and about six hands were held up
for it.

Mr. Gray wished to ask Mr. Broadhurst whether
the carpenters' committee had accepted the
agreement come to at the conference which had
been held betwoon the two eommittees.

Mr. Broadhurst said they had not done so.
Mr. Weighill said they wanted nothing to do
with the carpenters ; they had acted in their own
interests. They cared nothing about what the
carpenters thought.

Mr. Gray said he considered the carpenters had
been treated in a very discourteous manner by the
masons. As a mason ho would not now express
his opinion upon the agreement which had been
arrived at, but he thought it only fair that the
masons should suspend their decision until the
carpenters had time to consult together. The
masons had pledged their word to the carpenters'
delegates that they would act entirely with them.
Ho therefore moved—

That this meeting stand adjourned until the
committees of the masons and the carpenters have
had a further opportunity of conferring together.
The amendment WAS seconded from the body
of the hall, and upon being put to the meeting,
received about five votes.

The original resolution for tho adoption of the
report and agreement was then etrried almost
unanimously.

On Tuesday a large meeting of the masons was
held in the Sun Concert flail, Westminster-road,
for the purpose of bearing more full explanations
of the reasons which had induced the committee of
masons to enter into compromise with the masters'

committee than had been given at the meeting on
Saturday evening.
Mr. Broadhurst, who occupied the chair, with a
few introductozy remarks, entered into a long and
exhaustive defence of the arrangements which had
been made with the masters' committee. He con-
tended that such favourable terms would not have
been obtained by arbitration. He justified the
action taken by the masons' committee. He spoke
warmly against the carpenters' committee, by
whose premature action, on the Ist of June last,
the masons had been forced into their present
position. Again, the carpenters' committee had
succeeded in directing all outside subscriptions into
their coffers, and the masons had but little
pecuniary support to fall back upon. He hoped
the carpenters would accept the terms obtained by
the masons, as he was convinced they had neither
power nor influence to get any better. He con-
cluded a speech of more than an hour's length, by
announcing that the locked-out men would be paid
their second dividend on Wednesday morning.
He said that the acceptance of the arrangements
by the body of masons had boon transmitted to the
masters' secretary, and early action would no doubt
be taken thereon.

The masons' Wednesday meeting was held as
usual since the lock-out, at the Sun Concert Hall,
Mason-street, Westminster-road, and was even
more largely attended than usual, showing that
none of the men have gone to work.

Mr. Broadhurst, on taking the chair, expressed
his surprise at the committee not having received
any notice from the masters of the intention to
re-open the works that morning, and after some
discussion a resolution was proposed and carried:

That we, the masons, do not resume our work
until our committee receive an official notice from.
the Masters' Committee that the shops are ro-
opened.
A question was then asked as to what was to
be done with some half-dozen men who had gone
to work at Jackson and Shaw's, pending the
arrangement with the masters. The Chairman
said those men who had gone " black " would be
dealt with by the lodges to which they belonged ;
that meeting had no power to deal with them. At
a later period of the day, the official notice was
received by the committee, when another meeting
of the men was held in the evening, at which it
was resolved that work should be resumed.

articles.title: CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.
articles.text:
THE CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

The news of the arrangement etfact9d between
the masons and the masters' committee, reported
above, was very angrily received by the great
body of men who flocked to the committee-room at
the Brown Bear on Saturday night, to pay in the
levies towards the support of the men on strike and
locked-out. The wildest excitement possible raged,
and such expressions as "They al ways were a
cowardly, unreliable lot of black sheep," were very
general. Some.of those, however, who discussed
mutters calmly argued that such hours as those
agreed to by the masons would be most unoccept-
able to the carpenters, who wanted shorter hours
in the summer than in the winter, because they
were at close hard work in shops, frequently most
oppressive in the summer, and that they would
.
rather work longer hours by gas in the winter
months. The gonnal tone of the man was against
any compromise. The money was coining in very
fast. There were nine cashiers busy receiving
money from six to eleven as fast as they could
book it, and 'many of the men had to wait their
turns before they could pay it in. 'rho amount
received was about £3OO. There were about 1,833
men on the books, a large proportion of whom arc
society men, who front their own amalgamated
union receive 16s. per week strike pay, besides
about 7s. 3d. from the strike fund.

The shops were opened on Tuesday, not only
to the masons but to the members of the other
branches of the trade who choose to resume work
under the terms of the agreement entered into
between the employers and the operative masons ;
but the carpenters committee issued the follow-
ing notice which was placarded throughout the
metropolis :

Caution.—To Carpenters and Joiners.—The
central committee having received notice from the
committee of master builders that they intend
opening their shops to-morrow (12iresdiq) morning
to the men in all branches upon the tvrais agreed
to with the masons, atl carpenters and joiners are
hereby cautioned against entering any shop on
strike or lock-out upon any terms whatever until
aftcr the decision of the delegate meeting, which
will be held on Tuesday evening, at half-past
seven o'clock, at the Brown Bear.—By order of
the committee, Charles Alatk in, Sec., Brown Bear,
July Bth.

This, of course, prevented any men in the
carpentering trade who wished to act in unison
with their brethre,n (tom resuming work until
the decision of the delegate meeting was made
known.

At two o'clock on Monday afternoon, a general

meeting of the men on strike from Jackson and
Shaw's and Brass's firms was held at the Brown
Bear, Bloomsbury, to discuss the present position
of the dispute. After some discussion, a resolu-
tion was proposed and carried by an overwhelming
majority, condemnatory of the agreement with
the masons, and declaring adhesion to the terms
of the memorial. The meeting of the locked-out
men in the Pimlico district was also held on
Monday afternoon, when a resolution similar to
the above was unanimously adopted.

On Monday night a crowded meeting of the
delegates from the carpenters and joiners of
London was held at the Brown Bear, Bloomsbury,
to consider the measures necessary to be adopted
by the carpenters and joiners, in consequence of
the recent action taken by the masons. Mr. T.
Sadler occupied the chair.
The Chairman, on opening the proceedings,
said since the last meeting of delegates there had
been an important change in the position of the
look-out consequent upon the extraordinary con-
duct pursued by the masons. (Hear.) Ho then
wont on to detail the proceedings of the Masons'
Deputation and the Masters' Committee, which
have already been made public, He said without
hesitation the movement had been "sold" by the
masons. (Hear.) Let the masons resume work
if they please upon the terms they had arranged,
but the carpenters and the men of the other trales
would not follow the example. (Hear.) He was
firmly convinced that if the masons had stood side
by side with the carpenters for a short time longer,
the object for which they had all been struggling
would have been obtained. (Hear.) He then
read the resolutions adopted at the various district
committee-rooms, all condemnatory of the masons,
and calling upon the delegates to remain firm to
the terms of the memorial.
Mr. Sinclair moved the first resolution:—

That this meeting of delegates from the car-

TAB EAST-END TAILORS,
The very mention of East-end tailors will con-
jure up thoughts of sweating shops and consump-
tive skeletons plying needles to keep up the last
flicker of life in them. The tailoring trade has
Wormed itself in many respects under the vigi-
lant eye of workshop inspectors and the yearly-
ineressing demand for sewing labour. Formerly,
when a certain mischief-making personage ap-
peared among the tailors, it wes pretty certain to
he the earners of scanty wages who represented
themselves 44 ground down by middlemen. Now
the iiesition has changed, and the wage-receivers
have attained to comparative independence, while
the middlemen have gone to the wall. The sub-
contractor, or Imiddleman, is no capitalist beyond
owning a few machines, with most likely a` bill
of sale over them, and renting a workshop which
the law requires shall afford a certain amount of
space and ventilation to those whom he employs.
The single machine man will have to do his own
fitting and basting, and to employ two female
finishers besides the machinist. With two ma-
chines there will be a staff of eight hands, of
whom half-a-dozen will be females. This is
the average extent of a sub-contractor's estab-
lishment, and the maximum does not exceed
twenty or twenty-four hands. The subordinates
are all on day work, and have a regular standard
of twelve hours, beyond which they charge over-
time. The baster, who a few years ago thought
himself well paid with a pound a week, requires
now thirty shillings, and in many cases more.
The machinists vary, according to skill, from 245.
to 40s. a week; the highest rate being that now
demanded by efficient men, who are quite as ex-
tensively employed as women.
A. work. room for a machine party of four will
rent in the East-end at about 15s. per week; but
the average outlay in thia respect is from a pound
to thirty shillings a week. The materials are
given out by the warehouseraan, partially cut.
The sub-contractor has to fit them and pass them
on to the baiter, who prepares them for the
snachinist, from whom they finally proceed to the
finishers. Besides rent and gas—which they aay
has advanced 3d. per thousand in the East-end—
the seb-coatriestor must find his own thread and
all the implements required in his workshop.
Subject to these deductions, he undertakes to
make coats—double. breasted, half-lined, collared,
buttoned, and pocketed, at fifteen ponce each.
The thread alone costs lid., and the button-holes
6d. That is the lowest figure to which the sub-
contractor has yet been reduced; but 18d. for a
coat is no longer considered cutting too low. If
the work wore properly done in a West-end shop
It would occupy a man a day and a half, and

rise from 18d. to 25., and so on to 5a., which is
now a maximum amongst ready-made houses. A
great deal of the bespoke trade about the City and
in Oxford-street has drifted into a similar class of
*hops, but it manmade a slightly higher scale. A

Work is approved he may rise to Bs. The bespoke
trade, though apparently more profitable, hos its
drewbaeks. gentlemen who relish the idea of
ifetting a complete fit-out at three or four hours'

cial " is affixed to the garment specifying when it
must be returned. If not in to the minute, it is sent
for at the sub-oontractor's expense. If he fails 4
sewed time to keep his engagement, a more ex-
pensive messenger is despatched to him. The last

yery small fraction due upon the job. The best
clam of bespoke work whieh gets into the hands

4 coat. Trousers and vest* are comparatively less

articles.title: LONDON BAKERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON BAKERS.

The baking trade of London is in such a con-
dition, that it _may end one morning in finding us
broadless. Tho bakers have attempted a strike
several times during the past thirty years, but
they say they moan it seriously this time. The
one spare night in the week which they can call
their own they are devoting to the arrangement of
a programme.

The twelve hours principle stands foremost in
the bakers' chatter. It has been repeatedly
struggled for before—once six years ago, when
the trade was kept by it in a state of disaffection
for twelve months, and another time, twelve years
ago, when a partial strike wad made upon it in
some of the southern districts, There is better
hope for it now in consequence of the check that
has been given to German immigration by the
improved condition of the Germans at home, and
by the prohibition of juvenile labour which came
into force a few years ago. The Act which
forbade youths under eighteen years of age to be
employed in bakeries, raised the rate of wages of
beginners to 10s., and in cases 12s. a week. This
advance slightly bentilted the journeymen, though
their wages have been comparatively stationary for
the past ten years. In an ordinary shop, with three
or four hands, there would be a foreman earning
from 245. to 30s. a week, and a second hand
getting from 18s. to 255., and a third hand com-
mencing as low as Hs. A pound a week is the
average money pay of an efficient baker in London.

The diurnal routine of a baker's life begins
about six o'clock in the evening, when the poor
man has to set the sponge for the first batch. He
may have time then to go home and take a couple
of hours' sleep till fall work has to be started at
eleven o'clock. While the foreman seta the
sponge for the second batch, the other men ate
getting their dough out for the first. A batch
ranges from 150 to 180 loaves in plain baking,
but with fancy bread it has to be smaller. The
men say that these can be put through, an oven
comfortably in twelve hours, and hence their
standard of a day's work. At present, many shops
take four or five out of a single oven, which
tretches the day to fifteen or sixteen hours. If
the master has a weakness for earning a few
extra twopences by baking dinners, so much the
won() still for his men, To be ready for these
small commissions the oven has to be out of use
during severalhoura of the forenoon, consequently
the last batch cannot get throu_h till late in the

in the bakehouse 'till five or tiix o'clock in the
afternoon, and then had to recommence another
day's work at eleven o'clock. The pressure at the
end of the week in getting out a double supply of
bread for Saturday virtually knocks two days into
one. From the time of darting on Thursday night
till the bakery is cleared on Saturday afternoon,
there is hardly a wink of sleep for the baker nor a
minute to spare for his meals. After a few hours'
sleep he has to take his turn of Sunday duty at
roasting dinners. From half-past one o'clock on
Sunday afternoon to eleven o'clock at night is the
longest waking interval in the life of a baker free
from the responsibilities of yeast and dough.
Club meetings are to pave the way to some de-
cided action being taken by the bakers during the
coming week. Socially, the organisation is com-
plete, and the spirit of the men resolute, but there
does not seem as yet to have been a general plan
concerted. The Germans are strongly disposed to
do the thing comprehensively, and have notice
given to every baker in the metropolis for stopping
work by a certain date, should certain demands
not be complied with. These will comprise the
twelve hours first and foremost; after, the aboli-
tion of Sunday work; and, lastly, a higher scale
of wages. It is mooted that was 245. per week for
second hands and 30s. for foremen. Overtime is
not a prominent question, but it is recognised as a
necessity. The men would stipulate that it be
paid for, but they do not allude to exacting a
higher rate, or throwing any other obstacle in the
way of its practice.

articles.text:
THE AMALGAMATED TraINERS

SOCIETY.

On Tuesday evening a meeting of the members
of the above society was held at the Crown and
Can, St. John-street, Clerkenwell.
Mr. Dixon, secretary of the London district,
said he was glad to see the society increasing in
numbers so rapidly, and 1 e hoped be would soon
see the trade in an equal positioa to other trades,
and that could be done only by a thorough union
of all branches of the trade. lie then intro-
duced Mr. Ogden, the general secretary of the
union.

Mr. Ogden, who on rising was loudly cheered,
in the course of a long speech, said, like all other
societies when first starting, their numbers were
few, but now in six years they had increased to
such an extent they were able to effect a great
deal of good for both employers and employed, for
he did not believe any benefit could be maintained
except the interests 'of both were considered. He
was glad to see all branches of the trade were
taking up the question of unionism in London as
they bad done in his part of the country, Lanca-
shire, and he was confident that the North of
England turners would do all they could to help
their fellow craft in London and the South. He
asked every member to put his shoulder to the
work, and if all pushed on together success was
certain. Thanking them for the kind reception
they had given him and his colleague, Mr.
Horsfall, he resumed his seat amidst great
applause.
A vote of thanks to Mr. Ogden and Mr. Hors-
fall, which were duly responded to, closed the
meeting.

SATURDAY, JULY 13, 1872.

THE BISHOP AND THE AGITATORS.
Tint Bishop of PrrEnuonoucin has recently
been delivering himself on the Agricultural
Labourers' Strike, but, as might have been
expected from a bishop, without special refer-
ence to its cause, its probable consequences,
or to any practical method of treating it, with
a view to its settlement. A large number of
people have given their advice after the
manner of the BISIIOP, their only apparent
point being a condemnation of all outside
interference with special reference to agitators
who, according to these gentlemen are prowl-
ing about the country for the express purpose
of stirring up strife between the farmers and
the men, that they may make a profit of their
own evil work.
We have a right to expect more than this
from a bishop, if he in any way attempt to
touch the matter. Respectable advisers ef
the lay order should also do more than this.
The situation demands it; the peace of the
agricultural districts and the safety of pro-
perty in these districts demand it; and the
duty these persons owe to the country is not
discharged by a mere denunciation of agitators,
with whatever heartiness or ability this may
be done. Besides, these censures, to be use-
ful, ought to be made with strict and direct
reference to the • persons to whom they are
intended to apply, or they become altogether
useless, and in this sense we have a right to
ask the BrsnoP and others to whom they
refer, when they speak of agitators • creating
disturbance and danger from outside.
In plain truth they cannot do this, and in
attempting to shift the blame from the land.
lords and farmers, they are doing a cowardly
and dishonest work, and are seeking, in any-
thing rather than a creditable manner, to shirk
their own share: of a very serious responsi-
bility. There is ,no use in carping at
trifles, or insisting that the condition of Cho
agricultural labourer in nearly every one
of our English counties is about the lowest
condition of human existence. The. moral
and intellectual state of men, women,
and ohildren is most deplorable. Nothing
can be clearer than this. It is impossible
to go amongst them and speak to them
without being made aware of it, and we ask
Bishop MAGEE to account for this without
disparaging and disgracing the Church. We
ask the respectable denounoers of agitation to
account for it without self-accusation. Why
have they been living and looking •at this
horrible human slough without making some
manly, intelligent effort at effectual improve-
ment? Again; why have they been mouth-
ing piety and amassing wealth; literally,
truly, absolutely wallowing in wealth, whilst
these poor people have been hungering and
perishing for lack of the simplest necessaries
of life ?

It is impossible that these people can cheat
themselves into the belief that the agitation
amongstfarm labourers now going on is the
result, of outside interference, and not the
natural outcome of the neglected, degraded,
and suffering condition of the labourers. It
is asking the public to believe that mon,
women, and children would not be dis-
satisfied with an insufficiency of bad food
if somebody did not go amongst them to
tell them they ought to be so
that rags, and filthy smothering stys to
live in would not interfere with their content-
ment if outside agitators would not poke their
noses into the matter, Ana cry shame I Ac-
cording to this curious, but most reopectable
doctrine, it is not the reality that shocks or
hurts,
,but the representation of it. A men,
wording to this, may be kicked, and flogged,
and starved without knowing anything about
it if others do not tell him. That sensible and
well-meaning man, the Bishop of PETER.'
BOROUGH, could never be guilty of so impoliti°
an act as letting the "eat out of the bag" to
the disturbance of things as they are.
Tie
possesses some few thousands a year and
" perquisites; " he has no hungry children
crying to a heart-broken mother for bread
which she has not the means of giving them ;

his family are not robed in filthy rags, nor do
they sleep indiscriminately in fever-breeding
hovels; be can afford to be patient and
fashionably benevolent. So far as he is
concerned, things are very well. The Church,
of which he is so conspicuous an ornament,
has slumbered over this state of things with-
out interfering in a troublesome way between
the masters and the men, and the Church
would so slumber till the crack of doom, if
the poor sufferers did not cry out in their
agony, and if their fellow-workers in the
towns, disparaged as "unionists," did not show
earnestness in calling for the redress of the
wrong from which these poor men suffer.
But is not all this outcry against outside in-
terference the veriest cant that ever fell from
human lips? -Ulm what moral central idea
does our religion and civilization rest but that
of interfering to inform ignorance, to give
strength to weakness, to put right in the
place of wrong, to substitute truth for
error and happiness for misery? Of what
use is the Church, if human interference in
the cause of righteousness and justice is to be
rebuked? The existence' of a bishop as such
is an absurdity unless this he the case. The
work of Dr. MAGEE ought to be one of per-
petual interference, and every clergyman
under his control should be urged by him con-
.tinually to interfere until the disgraceful
barbarism, against which this labourers'
movement is a practical protest, be abated.
What are all our missionary societies but
associations for interfering in other people's
affairs? What an eloquent protest the
Bishop would make if the missionaries spread
throughout the world to produce dissatisfac-
tion with heathenism and barbarism were
'abused as "agitators," as stirrers up of
strife, as agents of mischief, working only
for the pounds and shillings whioh they
pocket thereby? Has our Baum, got it into
his., head that barbarism at a distance only
ought to be meddled with? Or does ho be-
lieve that what he andothers like him neglect to
do at home should not be interfered with? If so,
the sooner he gets such an idea out of his head
the better. There are other missionaries now
at work beside those who go to propagate the
Gospel in foreign parts, not in a spirit antago-
nistic to them, but rather in a spirit like unto
theirs, and this the BISHOP would soon dis-
cover were he as eager for the welfare of Eng-
land's field labourers as missionary societies
profess to be for that of interesting dark-
skinned heathens under the palm-trees of the
South. Let him not forget that the
farm-labourers have moved of themselves.
The half-dead, inert mass, has put itself
in motion, and there is no voice in the Church
or elsewhere that can from henceforth cora-
Mand it to be still. The Church, the land-
lords, the farmers are puzzled, and know not
what to say. The farmers feel they must
give higher wages, but:.comfort themselves by
thoughts of the revenge they, mean to take
when the winter mouths come round. The
landlords dwell in too bright and serene an
atmosphere to be as yet much troubled; whilst
the bishops, who arc always expected to say
something, mumble words of reproof to
"agitators."

If they are wise they will put an end to this,
and set about the work of reform themselves.
They can do it if they will, and if they
Will not, somebody must do it for them.
The nine or ten, or eleven shillings a-week,
with or without perquisites, has seen its end.
Men's hearts are stirred and their months aro
opened, and it would be as useless to attempt
to prevent the consequenoes as it would be to
try to attempt to conjure the sun into a
snuff-box. The idea of union has got
thoroughly in amongst the farm labourers,
and it has done too much already in advancing
wages not to be cherished and extended.
From the Leamington centre real farm
labourers have been sent out to propagate
the idea of union to "foreign parts," in
Dorset and Somerset. Volunteer agencies
are also at work, and the simple truth that it
is better in a good cause to act together than
alone, will, in the country, as in the towns,
take possession of the minds of men never
more to be given up under any plea, pretence,
or inducement whatsoever, and the great duty
of farmers, landlords, and bishops shoulci be

to find out how they can accept this in a kindly
and peaceful spirit, and work with it to the
profit of the nation.

FRENCH SAVINGS BANKS,

M. DE LAMAUCE, in an article on savings-
banks in the Revue des Deux Mondes; gives
the following account of the manner in which
the Paris Savings-bank bore the trial to which
it was exposed during the first and second siege
of Paris :

The affair of the savings-banks during
the siege of Paris (says this writer) forms
one of the most curious and most edifying
pages in the history of our time. It is, thanks
to the workmen depositors of Paris, that the
institution of savings-banks in France may
henceforward be said to be proof against any
trial, for what trial could be feared of greater
violence and duration? At the time of tho
execution of the decree of the 17th of
September, 1870 (limiting payments in specie
to 60 francs, the rest to be paid in bills
on the Treasury), the Paris Savings-bauk
reckoned 245,000 depositors: at 50 francs in
specie to each deposit-book there was a sum
of from 10 to 12 million francs which could be
claimed. Now, in the first month, in October,
the payments in specie amounted to 300,000
francs, and in spite of the decrees and minis-
terial decisions which kept up the monthly
payments on account of 50 francs per deposit-
book, the total of payments in specie up to the
31st of March, 1871, during six months,
amounted only to 1,750,000 francs; the dis-
bursements of the Treasury are even reduced
to one million, if the 750,000 francs paid in
by the depositors in the same six months be
taken from the 1,750,000 re-imbursed. As to
bills on the Treasury, they were delivered to
depositors for 447,000 francs. Thus the
Treasury paid out less than one million and
a-half francs from October to March to meet
demands upon a balance of forty-four million
francs. It must be acknowledged that the
Treasury extricated itself from the situation
without much expense or trouble, and to the
satisfaction of those interested.

The Commune, that is to say the second
siege of Paris, from the 18th of March to the
28th of May, modified the movement of re-
demption in a slight degree only. The
reimbursements continued on the basis of the
monthly decrees; from the Ist of April they
were :-41,000 francs, 46,000 francs, 67,000
francs, 39,000 francs, 68,000 francs, 40,000
francs, 30,000 francs; on the 20th of May,
the eve of the decisive struggle, 74,000
francs; the 27th of May during the struggle,
1,672 francs only; an immediate increase
on the 3rd of Juno, 54,000 francs. By a
clever precaution, the administration of the
savings-bank had in its current account with
the Bank of France secured a higher balance
than usual; it drew on this for its operations
in specie; but the service of the Treasury
bills and the purchases of interest had to
cease from the 2nd of April. The savings-
banks remained open and continued to receive
sums paid in. These sums, indeed, dimi-
nished rapidly: here are the figures in thou-
sands of francs from the 18th of March-
-87,000 francs, 36,000 franos, 27,000 francs,
17,000 francs, 6,000 frame, 7,000 francs,
3,000 francs, 4,000 francs, 4,000 francs, 3,000
francs; 3,461 francs on the 27th of May, and
725 francs on the 3rd of June. From the
10th of Juno, the amount paid in rose to
18,544 francs.
Order having been restored, the Govern-
ment and the /National Assembly resolved to
show their esteem and benevolent regard
for the depositors of the savings-banks by
granting them a favour—the law of the 21st
of June, 1871, authorised them to demand
the conversion of their deposits into 5 per
cent " rentes," on the conditions of the sub-
scription to the loan of the 23rd of June.
They were allowed four days in which to
announce their intentions. The Savings-bank
of Paris received 4,309 demands for conversion,
the capital converted amounted to 2,096,747
francs 90 centimes. A few days after this,
the law of the 12th of July, 1871, abrogated
all the restrictions imposed in consequence
of the decree of the 17th of September, 1870,
and the savings-banks resumed their statutory
action,

To speak definitely, the stock of the Paris
Savings-bank, reckoned at 54 millions before
the war, went down to 41 millions on the 17th
September, 1870, to 41 millions in June, 1871,
and to 39 millions after the conversion
authorized for the loan of the 23rd of June,
1871 ; it was, at last, reduced on the 31st of
December, 1871, to 37 millions by the result
of the general exhaustion of means, and by
the resumption of labour when the small
tradesmen and manufacturers had to meet
their renewed bills, their rent, and the pur-
chase of raw material or goods. This exhaus-
tion of the last savings, aggravated by taxes,
continued during the first months of the
current year. Thus much for Paris. What
happened in the rest of France?

In July, 1870, before the war, the balance
of all the savings-banks of France, including
Paris, amounted to 720 millions, represented
by 500 millions at interest, and 220 millions
current account at the Treasury. The depart-
mental savings-banks, less fortunate than those
of Paris, or less well-defended in default of a
superior commission of French savings-banks
connected with Government, endured the full
rigour of the decree of the 17th of September,
1870; the depositors had only a right, once
for all, to 50 francs each deposit-book, and
for the rest to bills on the Treasury. This
system of exception was continued down to
the 17th of July, 1871. They had no alle-
viation except by the law of the 21st of June,
1871, which, to serve the loan of the 23rd of
June, offered an advantageous conversion into
5 per cent " rentes " : 64 millions were thus
converted in the whole of France, including
Paris.

The stock of the French savings-banks was
reduced in March, 1872, to 526 millions, in
diminution of 104 millions on the stock
previous to the war. That is 'a reduction of
nearly a quarter for the departments; the
reduction for Paris in scarcely a third, although
at Paris the Treasury offered monthly sums
of 50 francs on account during ten months,
sufficient to exhaust almost all the deposit
books. Hence the Parisian depositors, more
satisfied with the proceedings of Government,
showed themselves relatively more discreet
than the provincial depositors in their demands
for reimbursement. The system of fractional
and periodical reimbursements practised at
Paris during the crisis, was, therefore, as
happy a solution for the Treasury as for
the depositors, as good for the credit of the
State as for the popularity of the savings-
banks. There is a precedent which resolves
one of the capital questions of the institution
of savings-banks, reimbursement in times of
crisis. We must, however, acknowledge that
these unforeseen measures, these decrees for
partial reimbursement, striekly speaking,
constitute a violation of the contract inscribed
in the organic law of savings-banks with
regard to the depositor.
M. DE LAMARCE recommends, therefore,
that the organic law should in future contain
an accessory clause giving the State power to
reimburse claimants to a certain extent by
similar means in times of panic, and civil dig-
turbanee.

articles.title: VOTE TO EYRE.
articles.text:
THE VOTE TO EYRE.

MR. EYRE and his friends may be made
welcome to whatever comfort they can extract
from the reasons assigtied by the PRIME
MINISTER for putting the vote before the
Committee of the House of Commons. Over
and over again in the discussion to which it
gave rise, the brand of " Murder" was
affixed to all who had any hand in the death
of Mr. GORDON and similar atrocities. The
camp at Satory is not the only spot in the
world which may claim the red title of
Aceldatna." " The motion," said Mr.
GLADSTONE, "which governed us in asking the
House for a sum of money, was the circum-
stance that we found what we deemed to be
a substantial engagement to Govern or EYRE
from our predecessors, and that we felt our-
selves bound in honour and policy to fulfil that
engagement." The member for North Stafford-
shire said the course was a shabby one, and
complained of their want of courage in not
stating their opinions on the merits. Did it
never occur to him that their reason for saying,
little on the merits might have been that they

would have been compelled to treat tlem in a
way not agreeable to his client? Whatever
conclusion they might have came to on the
merits, they certainly could not have come to it
in the spirit or with the disposition of casting
reproaches upon those' who arrived at an
opposite result. But if the question had been
free from all considerations of prior engage-
ment, they would not have thought it their
duty to be the authors of such a proposal.
Mr. GL.tnsroNli gave the history of the
previous engagement. The late Government
announced to Mr. EYRE, that, when the trial
, had concluded, and they had considered the
evidence, they would proceed to further
question whether they would pay the whole
or a portion of the costs. The trial reaches its
conclusion, the Government considers the
evidence, and Mr. Entor is directed. by the
Duke of BUCKINGTIIII to request that Mr.
EYRE will furnish a statement of the costs of
his defence. Having given that intimation, it
was not until the 6th of November that any
further definitive act was taken by the Govern-
ment in the case. Then comes another letter
clenching the engagement. The Si?.CRETA.RY to
the TREASURY writes to the SOLICITOR to the
TREA.SURY : "I desire that you will put your-
self into communication with the solicitor to
Mr. EYRE, as suggested in the Colonial-office
letter of the 3let of July, and advise my lords
as to the amount to be defrayed by her
lIIJESTY'S Government." The only further
question is, whether the injunction was im-
mediately obeyed, and the Solicitor, writing
under date of 22nd. April, 1869, says—" In
obedience to their lordships' command, I put
myself immediately into communication with
Mr. EYRE'S solicitor, requesting to see his
bills of costs." It is impossible to doubt that
a full and perfect engagement has been formed.
But, though the engagement had boon
formed. by the late Government, it had, not
been fulfilled. It remained, therefore, for the
consideration of their successors whether the en-
gagement was one which they were bound filth°
usual way to fulfil. On this head also Mr. GLAD-
STONE'S explanations were clear. While admit-
ting the difficulties, and neither claiming any
credit nor casting any blame upon others, tliey
yet considered that they should best discharge
their obligation to the country by giving the
Rouse of Commons that opportunity of fairly
examining and weighing the whole matter to
which they were entitled. It was said by one
speaker that they endeavoured to dispose of
this by a technical consideration between the two
Governments. It was not as a matter of honour
towards the former Government, but as a
matter of honour towards Mr. EYRE, and, in
accordance with the general principles on
which the public service is and must be
conducted. The fad that this vote had been
passed by two Governments did not in the
slightest degree bind the House of Commons.
Whether adopted or rejected, it would be done
by the perfectly free, -unbiassed, and indepen-
dent judgment of the House.
Mr. RUSSELL GURNEY said all that could
he said in mitigation of the case against Mr.
EYRE, and the speech of Mr. R. M. FowLER
was wonderfully merciful towards him, after
the manly condemnation pronounced by Mr.
GILPIN, another member of the Society of
Friends; but, with the Pam MINISTER sig-
nificantly declining to go into the merits of
the case, and the largo minority of 130
against the vote, Mr. EYRE derives little
moral benefit from the result; and, as to the
mere money, where would he have been had
not the Opposition, over ready to give away
other people's cash, come to the rescue?

articles.title: DISPUTE IN THE BUILDING TRADES,
articles.text:
THE DISPUTE IN THE BUILDING
TRADES,

WE are satisfied that in a short time the
strike—for the lock-out has now eeased—will
settle itself. We shall not examine its policy
or conduct until it has been brought to a close,
as neither the present position of parties, nor
the temper of the men engaged, gives promise
that anything useful could be produced by the
very best advice that could be given.
There are two lessons, however, which are
as plain now as they can be made by anything
yet in reserve, and these we
as they cannot be studied
sthhaeufpuotuitrite
out
ts
here,
or turned to profit too soon. The first is the
value of arbitration, as comparet with strikes

10

and lock-outs. Who can doubt after what'
has transpired with the masons that all which
has been gained might not have been obtained
without any serious disturbance in the build-
ing trade? Or who can for a single instant
refuse to believe that if the thousands
of men •on strike had obtained the
concessions now accepted without ceasing
work, and losing wages, the advantages would
have been entirely on their, side. It may be
repeated that victory won in a trades
,struggle
is not a permanent gain; whilst concession&
by mutual agreement carry the chief conditions
of permanence in them, and continually in-
crease the good feeling between employers and
employed, which in the end will most
assuredly ripen into a thorough mutual trust.
No time should be now lost in organizing a
board of arbitration for the building trades.
The necessity for, such a tribunal has been
proved, its utility, and necessity are _beyond
question, and on the principle that a good
thing cannot be done,too soon, we request the
intelligent working men of the building trades
to take this excellent work up without further
delay.

The second lesson is the necessity which has
been proved for a grand Amalgamatid. Union
in the building trades. That existing in the
iron trades demonstrates the practical value.
of such an organization; whilst the miserable
want of a cordial understanding in the present
strike between the trades engaged on it most
directly interested, painfully points to a defi-
ciency which should no longer be allowed to
exist. Small jealousies and mean fends
should not be permitted to stand in the way
of a noble work. And what work can have
in it a nobler purpose than that which leads
to a perfecting of that organization of in-
dustry which shall reconcile and harmonize
the interests of a great indhstrial country
such as England? Amalgamation in trades
where their operations run into each other is
a far higher form than isolation. Discordant
counsels and divergent action are almost in-
evitable where separate bodies try to act in
unity. And, without wrong intention, mere
liability to misunderstanding will sometimes
produce strife where it is both the interest and
intention of the men to act fairly and con-
siderately towards each other. The Amalga-
mated Engineers have solved the difficulties,
and realized the advantages belonging to such
a form of association. They have regulated
the interests and action of the different trades
that compose their great union. They have
unity of thought, harmony of action, and
power of numbers, without the danger of
disagreement or mutiny when the day
of trial comes ; and if .the building trades
after the experience of the last few weeks,
and the divisions and jealousies which
have existed, and which now exist, do not see
this, they have less clearness of vision than
*e at present giio them credit for.

No doubt this proposition will take time to
realize, There are many things to be arranged
before it can be carried out, even though it
was cordially and generally acoepted. It is
.a
work, nevertheless, to be considered, and, if
approved of, set about and accomplished)
whatever obataeles have to be overcome, or
whatever oppositien may be given to it by
those prejudieed in favour of limited local
action.

THE PAPAL POLICY IN ITALY.
AN apparent change of policy is taking
place at Rome. We say apparent, because at

The change of poliey td whieh all these re.

can be returned,- but "given to persons most

himself to a deputation of the. parish priests Of

one last effort to save the country and the

ing with themselves the example set by

articles.title: BALLOT SAFE.
articles.text:
THE BALLOT SAFE.

THE I.Clllf3e of Lords has justified our prog-
nostications, that the Ballot was safe. The
majority of the Peers have wisely shrunk
from the complete nullification and consequent
denial of a measure desired by the people and
granted by their representatives. The PRIME
MINISTER was firm on the main point. He
distinctly declared that nothing should induce
,him to wept the optional principle which had
been applied to the measure. The majority of
nineteen, composed of moderate and really
sagacious Peers, have saved the country from
a political crisis in which the hereditary
chamber would have had nothing to hope but
much to fear. The opponents of secret voting
had contrived to collect a number of petitions
in support of their views, in the preparation,
adoption, and. signing of which, the
principle of publicity of which they profess to
have so much at heart, had been avoided with
such perfect care, that until the fact of their
presentation by individual Peers became
knewn through the morning journals, the ex
istence of such things was as secret as the grave.
The Duke of RicnotoNn, who had been seen
in close consultation with Mr. DISRIELI just
before the question came on, has, however,
been disvowed as leader of the majority. He
was unable to obtain the aid, of Earl GREY,
who refused to be. party to an amendment
alestruetive of the measure; while the Duke
of NORTIIITMBERLAND, no friend to it by any
means, fairly broke away, telling Mr. DISRAELI
in round terms that it had been made neces-
sary by his own rash effort to get political
capital cut of Parliamentary Reform, "it
seemed to him," hesaid, "that a very stria
system of Hecreey was necessary for the pro-
tection of the voter from the tyranny of the
mob." We lOU not debate with his Grace who
Will oompoae the mob and who will set them on.
Enough for us, that the probability of attempts
to intimidate is conceded, and that a strictly
secret system of voting is. admitted to be the
only effectual protection.
Lord Canals, and even the Marquis of
SALISBURY, were silent; and the division
would have been taken. without a debate but
for Earl Rusaux, who, in a "rest and be
thankful spirit, warmly resented the notion
of anything being wanted to complete the
work of Reform beyond what is historically
connected with his own name. The amend-
ment making the Bill temporary instead of
permanent was re-affirmed ; but the impor-
tance of that point is secondary, No true
friend- to the Ballot is afraid of its being
made experimental, so long ae the experiment
is fairly tried ; Witt eight years is not a closely
limited period.

MENITING AT DILSTON.

On Wednesday evening a meeting of miners was
held at the Temperance Hall, 13ilston, for the pujr-
pose of meeting a deputation of miners who waited
upon the masters the same day in Wolverhampton.
There was a large attendance, and the decision

That the workinq hours should be from six I
o'clock in the morning until thiee o'clock, p.m.,

Considerable dissatisfaction was expressed at
the decision, and it was unaiiiiuoysly resolved

OPEN.AIII MEETING AT DRIDPOILT.
An enthusiastie meeting wad held on Priddy
evening last in afield opposite the Gas Works,
Bridport. Mr. George s Potter, Mr. Mitchell,
London; Mr. Lloyd Jones, 3. Mitchell, Esq., J.
Plummer, F,sq., Messrs. Arlington and Harris,
from Warwickshire, and the committee occupied
a waggon provided with seats. About 4,000
-- people , were present, a large number being
labourers.

, Mr. Potter on presen,ting himself was received
with loud cheer, and opened the proceedings ía a
speech of considerable interest, and which is fully
reported in the Bridport Kews and Pulmam's
!Freckly Taper.
, ILI read the following letter, received from Mr.
T 4 A, Mitchell, member for the borough, in answer
to an invitation to attend the .meeting sent by the
Workman's Committee .

. have paid fall .attention to your letter
of the 4th of June, and can hava no hesitation in
assuring you of. my sympathy with the efforts
originated at Leamington, and prosecuted in
various other districts by the agricultural labourers
to raise their condition. Certainly at the present
moment it is far too depressed, and subscriptions
may be fairly asked to enable them to emigrate
from one part of the kingdom to another; where
better wages. prevail. • In this way Something
nearer approaching to a. level may be finally
attained. Before sending you any money, how-
ever, I Should like
.tO have faller information of
the rules, objects, and intentions of the association,
because, as you observe, very few of the class live
in Bridport. If the different phases.of the trades
unions are to be established there they may extend
tiz the manufacturers of the town, and with 'my
knowledge of the severe competition* with Scot-
land,- and of the; general well-being of the town,
I do not consider such a 'proeeeding necessary at
present. Waiting to hear further from you, I am,
•• yours. respectfully, T. A. MITCHELL.
The Chairman then introduced......
Mr. George Mitchell, of 'London, who was re-
ceived with loud cheers. lie said that he had
been called a stomper lie was, he supposed, at
nineteen years of age, one of the most ignorant
young men to be found, for he could not tell ."
a
girt A from a bull's focit." Ilerwished, if there
. .
- were any head 'carters 'present, to ask them a

(Laughter.) ' But he neier allowed the head

(Laughter.) Ile used to plough from hedge to

had challenged the farmers of that parish to

spirit or pluck to take him up. (Cheers). Some
of the labourers of Bridport. had asked him to
como down. Ile said to them, "1 suppose you

will pay for the bills and the expenses of getting
up the meeting." They replied, "We have not
got 'a penny in the - world." He answered,
"Very well, then, get out the hills and I will pay
the expenses." -He vvaa literally starved away
from Montaeute. He had loaded hay until ten
and eleven o'clock at night—when his father and
mother had gone to bed—and had only a half-
penny dishful of cold " tadies" add a httle salt
for his supper, having had nothing in him all day

physic when they drank cider. (Cheers.) He
did not come down to advocate the cause of the
man who would go to sloop en the suit handles*
He should be sorry to do such a thing. He was
there to advocate the cause of the honest, hard-
working, industrious man who was underpaid,
and whom the farmers know was uederpaid.
Some farmers had talked to him privately and

fact, and said also that the wages of the labourer
must be raised. Whet he said to the farmers wai
you have kept back the
this—" If for 25 years

hire of the labourer, it is but fair and honest that
you should give him in a lump sum the amount
'which you etiglitio have paid him." (I voice—
They have betight two or "three hunters with that
'money.) He. was not in favour of Strikes,
There were some farmers who said, "I will give

.seemed as if the
world was up in arms against them: No liberal

to them,
.but why did they not tell the farmers

He had heard Methodist parsons couiplaining that
nien.Aid not attend prayer meetings. Why was it P
Beeanse the poor fellows, having werked all the
"Week, Were unfit to go to church or to fill up the
pews' of the chapel. They appeared not to have

•(Applause.)
Mr. Mitchell then stated that he had many a time

(Voices —"They go to the parish.") lle hoped

John Phippen then moved the following reso-

11.,8o1ved, that in the opinion of this meeting
