MEZTINO AT CIiEWKERISTE.

Mr. G. Potter, Mr. Mitchell, Mr. Lloyd Sono,
and the delegates from Warwickshire, attended
meeting in. the Market Squ.are, Crowicerne, on
Saturday evening. A platform bad boon erected
opposite the George LTotel. Between 1,000 and
2,000 persons were present; the push of hay-
making doubtles.s kept many uway,
Upon the motion of Mr. George Mitchell,
seconded by Mr. Lloyd Jones, Ur. Potter took the
chair.

The Chairman having opened the proceeding is
in a suitable spech, which is fully reported in the
local paper,

Mr: Lloyd Jones said thnt he wanted to speak
upon that subject in coonootica with the general
movement going on in theconotry. The question
was of great interest to all who considered the
future prosperity of the country. In all the largo

--
towns, where industrial occupations were carried
on, where the artizans were skilled men, the con-
tention of labour and capital had been going on

fora considerable number of years. Trades

unions, which were mentioned there perhaps for
the first time, were in the manufacturing districts
very old institutions. The men by combination
bad given themselves a strength which they never
could have possessed without it, and employprs,

knowing that that strength existed, and knowing
also, whether they conquered or were being con-
quered by it, that it was a dangerous thing to
grapple with, had come to that method of peace-
able settlement which neighbouring nations

adopted when they found their powers evenly
balanced—believing that a reasonable settlement
was better than a settlement by warfare. If any
number of men were to enter into a union, into a
conspiracy, or whatever they liked to call it, and
determine that they would be absolutely con-
tented with their position, that every one of them
would vow not to ask for a fraction more than they
received, and that their children should not be
educated, that would be a union which could not
by any possibility keep in existence. The very
fact of the advancement going on amongst all
classes of the country would compel them to be-
come active, to move with the rest of their fellow
countrymen, and be participators in the growing
prosperity of the country. (Cheers.)

The Chairman then introduced Mr. Mitchell, of
London. In doing so he was interrupted by several
young men in front of the George Hotel laughing,
and he observed that the meeting was too serious
to be pooh-poohed by a lot of puppies. (Cheers.)
Mr. Mitchell was received with cheers. It wai
quite evident that the laughers were the winners.
(Cheers.) They had been squeezing the poor in
a mut rascally manner. He had taken a deal of
trouble to get the six gentlemen who repre-
sented Somerset to be present there that
evening. Ho had written again and again
and could not obtain an answer from one of
them. Previous to the meetings at Monte
-
cute and Chard he wrote courteously, as
became one from the plough. He wrote again,
but no answer arrived. He thought it seemed
strange, and he instructed his clerk to enclose a
stamped directed envelope,put a piece of paper in-
side the envelope and to write again. He received
answers from five out of the six. (Laughter.) If
any commercial man sent to him a directed en•
velopo inside of a letter he thought at once there
was something up. He did not think that was a
proper way to treat commercial men. He was a
commercial man, and if any mrin could say that he
played second fiddle to any man in the same busi-
ness in Europe let him say it. (Cheers.) And he
had ploughed an acre of ground for 3d., and that
within six miles of that spot. Who had reaped
the benefit of that? " Maaster." Mr. Mitchell
then narrated the incident that made him leave
Montacute, and spoke of the inability of
tradesmen to support the movement. Ile ob-
served that one of the county members wrote
to him to the effect that he did not think be (Mr.
Mitchell) was going to do any good in Somerset.
He (the member) was afraid of offending the
farmers, fearing that he might lose their votes.
He did not say so, but there was no doubt that
was the reason he did not take up their cause. The
time would come when he would do so, and say,
"We have done this for the men." Why did he
not come out in the front? That was the time—
now or never. He would tell them an anecdote.
Ho remembered once taking his father's breakfast
—a pot full of teakettle broth. (Laughter.)
When the breakfast was given to his father he
put it down and commenced pulling off his coat.
He (Mr. Mitchell) said to him, "Father, what are
you going to do now?" "Why," he replied,
"I am going to swim after the saps, to be sure."
(Loud laughter.) If they could got the spoon to
stand upright it would be all well. His object in
coming there was to bettor their cause. Ho would
scorn the idea of coming for his own benefit. The
slaves in South America were better off than the
labourers in the West of England. Even the
Mahommeclans were better paid, and the Russian
serfs were hotter housed and better clad than the
labourers generally. They had plenty of bread.
They were bigger men than those he saw before
him, for they had more victuals. He knew that
Somerset labourers had not enough to eat. Mr.
Mitchell then spoke of labourers' clothing, and
stated that the reason many of them did not go to
a church or chapel on Sundays was owing to their
not having clothes to wear. If they had good
clothes they would be as proud to wenr them as
some of those laughing gentlemen. On Sundays
the spirit seemed to be gone out of the men into
the farmers' pockets. (Laughter.) Many a man
had to go to bed whilst his Hiatt was washed. Ile
had himself done so many times. Mr. Mitchell then
alluded to Will Chant, one of the men examined

at Moutacute. He was described in the Times as

a very old man. But he was only nine months

older than himself, and ho (Mr. Mitchell) should
undoubtedly have looked older if for 27 years

he had vvoiked for those laughing gentlemen
opposite. His desire was that the labourers should
be elevated and more respectable. He believed
that the more respectable a man was the more his
master would like him. How could hobo respectable
if he could not buy clothes? They bought some
of the tallyman occasionally, but he was always
knocking at the door. (Laughter.) Some of the
great people and farmers—God bless them for not
having more brains—said, "If you give the
labourers more wages they will go to the public-
house." What a lame excuse. Did they mean to
say that because they had 15s. a week they would
spend more at the publichouse ? He had a bettor
opinion of the labourers. There might be a few,
but he would not condemn the whole. He would
not deprive the honest upright working man of his
rights. If the labourers drank as much brandy
as the farmers it would kill them—(laughter)—
for, unlike the masters, they had no mutton chops
for the brandy to feed upon. If they joined the
labourers' union they would be protected by each
other, and notbeat the mercy of the workhouse. Mr.
Mitchell then referred to bread, and commented
upon the practice of not weighing it to the
purchaser. He then passed on to the question of
the farmers not affording to pay higher wages. Ho
knew a farm of 500 acres not many miles off. The
cost of labour only amounted to £3OO a year, and
the farmer pocketed £1,500. In 1 824 two farmers
entered the parish referred to in straitened cir-
cumstances. It was stated:that they only had one
shirt between them. They worked bard, but at
the end of thirty yours one of them could buy his
farm four times over. He (Mr. Mitchell) did not
envy the man, for he believed that he was as
miserable as a grave digger. (Laughter.) The
man who defrauded the labourer of his hire could
not be happy. He could pick out ten families in
Montacuto reared upon smith averaging not a
halfpenny a head each. A gentleman had written
to the papers to the effect that the labourer's
position was improved, for the females had the
opportunity of earning 10s. a week at gloving.
He got the women together, and they told him
that their earnings did not exceed on the average
2s. 6d. a week. •

At this stage the fire-bell at the Town Hall
sounded, and the cry of " Fire" was raised.
Many of the audience rushed away, and great
confusion and alarm was caused. The ringing
was the act of some idiot who thought thereby to ;
break up the meeting, and who ought to be '
punished for the alarm and disturbance so foolishly
caused. It is no credit to an individual or to a
town in resorting to such means of stifling public
discussion, however unpalatable the subject.
After the hooting and groaning which testified the
feelings of the audience bad terminated,
Mr. Mitchell continued, and referred to the
statement made that the labourers of Montacute
had meat cooked in the bakehouses every Sunday.
He went to the bakehouses and found that only
four labourers had meat. One had a "joint" of
the value of 6d., with potatoes, and he would not
have had that but for being turned out of his
situation for joining the union, and being pre-
sented with half-a-sovereign. (Laughter and
cheers.) A second bad half a sheep's head, a
third two pennyworth of fat, and a fourth about a
halfpenny worth of fat—the value of the whole
of the dinners was not worth 2s. So much for
the beef and " fined " pudding. Mr. Mitchell
concluded by expressing a hope that the time
would come when the labourers would be able to
have meat for their dinners, and their condition
improved. (Cheers.)
The Chairman said he could not call upon the
labourers from Warwickshire to move a resolution
without from that public platform denouncing in
the strongest manner the despicable conduct of the
Persons who rang the flre-bell. (Hisses, groans,
and disorder.) Whether they were boys or men
it mattered not. It was a foolish act, and done
for a purpose. (hear, hear, and cheers.) it
deserved the strongest condemnation, and he
hoped and trusted the representative of the press
would give it as such. (Cheers.) They were
there as working men to state their case,
and were not to be put down. They would come
there again, and so agitate the neighbourhood that
the whole town should gather round them and
' denounce the conduct of 'those foolish farmers.
(Cheers.)
Mr. Allington, Warwickshire, then moved the
following resolution
That in the opinion of this meeting
the arongest encouragement should be given
to the present movement amongst the agri-
cultural labourers in favour of unions and an
advance in wages, and that this meeting urges
the necessity of the labourers of the district to at

once form a branch of the National Argrieultural
Union.
He was a labourer and knew their griev-
ances. But there was set on foot a system
calculated. to elevate them, nothwithstanding op-
pression, and that was the National Agricultural
Union. If ho could prove that the union would
not injure any man, but would benefit the
labourer, then he should prove that it was a good
thing. Their object was not to injure any man.
Mr. Thomas Harris, in seconding the resolution,
said that the labourers had not received fair
remuneration for their work—not, enough to
provide comfortably for their families. He then
showed that a family could not live at a penny a
meal for less than 83. 9d. a week--to say nothing
of rent, clothes, and necessaries. They had
commenced the battle and intended to go for-
ward. Napoleon said that the English were lions
abroad but donkeys at home. The labourers had
been donkeys, for they had borne every burden
put upon them. But the farmers had at last
screwed a little too hard, and they wore now
awaking to their real position. Mr. Might had
triumphed, but Mr. Right would take his place.
He concluded 6. speech of considerable power by
expatiating upon the benefits to be derived from
union.

M. Thomas Saint, a labourar, of Crewkerne.
also addressed the meeting. He thought that it
was time the subject should be brought before the
public. At the last general election he referred to
the labour question. At that time labourers were
only getting front 7s. to Bs. a week. The wages
had, be believed, now risen to Os. a week. On the
previous Monday ho took a walk to Misterton,
and spoke to a man who was mowing. The man
told him that he had been working from four
o'clock in the morning, and had had nothing to
oat but a piece of dry broad. The man at last
became so fatigued that he
.was obliged to leave
work. That was a man willing to work but
unable to do so for want of food. He knew that
the labourers had not sufficient wages, and hoped
that all would become members of the mail.
The resolution was carried unanimously.
Three cheers were then given for the farmer
who should first raise the wages of his men—for
Mr. and Mrs. Mitchell, and for Mr. Potter, and
the proceedings terminated.
MEETING AT SEVENOAKS.

A large meeting, convened under the auspices
of the National Union, was held at Sevenoaks,
Kent, on Friday evening last. The meeting was
for the purpose of forming a branch of the
National Union for the district, and was said to be
held in direct opposition to the wishes of the Kent
Agricultural Labourers' Union, between whom
and Warwickshire a difference has arisen. War-
wickshire, it appears, has recently invited several
branches of the Kent Union to disunite from their
county Union and to join the National; and to this
the great body of the Kent men object. Mr.
Simmons, the promoter and hon. secretary of the
Kent Union, attended the meeting, and protested
against the conduct of Warwickshire in having
caused a division in the Kent Union, by inducing
individual branches to join .the National, instead
of officially inviting the whole Union to do so, so
that the matter could be fairly discussed.
Mr. Herbert, M.P., was in the chair on behalf
of the National Union, but refused to allow Mr.
Simmons to address the meeting. It appears that
the Kent Union is not opposed to a National
Union, but they objeot to sending the whole of
their funds to Warwickshire, and consider that the
control over the management of the funds afforded
to the counties is insufficient.

articles.title: LOCK-OUT Or LABOURERS IN OIFORDSIIIRE.
articles.text:
LOCK-OUT Or LABOURERS IN OIFORDSIIIRE.

The first instance of active opposition to the
Labourers' Union has occurred at Woolton, Ox-
fordshire, on the Duke of Marlborough's estate.
The union district secretary gave notice that the
labourers would require after last week union
hours and wages. The farmers immediately
formed a counter organization, and mutually
agreed not to employ any unionist, and to make
good any malicious injury they might sustain in
consequence. Last Saturday they accordingly
locked out all labourers, upwards of 100, connected
with the union. This step was loudly condemned
at the labourer's meeting on Saturday night.
The National Agricultural Union will support the
labourers if the farmers -persist.

THE NINE HOUR MOVEMENT IN

CANADA.

AN APPEAL TO THE WORKING CLASSES OF ENGLAND.
For a considerable time a growing agitation has
been in progress among the working men in Canada
for the purpose ofsecuring a reduction in the hours ;
of labour; and while watching with a keen and
lively interest the progress of the short time move-
ment in Britain, they have been diligently organ-
izing and preparing for the accomplishment of the
same reform here.
Believing that your sympathies will be cordially
extended to your brethren on this side of tbe
Atlantic, we venture to present you with a brief
delineation of our present difficulty.
The printers and bookbinders of the City of
Toronto presented a memorial to their employers,
requesting the adoption of 54 hours as constituting
a week's work, giving valid reasons why the re-
quest was neither injudicious nor ill-timed. Their
request met with a contemptuous denial, and the
men struck work. During the first three weeks
of the strike, the master printers resorted to threat.,
intimidation, and bribes to break up the union
among the men. Failing in these attempts, they
brought individual printers before a pliable police
magistrate, and obtained sentence against them
upon the plea that they had left their work with-
out giving due notice thereof, :the custom of the
trade and of the country being for both employer s
and employed to give era take a minute's notice.
Finding even this to fail in breaking up the union,
they have at last caused to be arrested twenty-
four members of the Typographical Union, upon
the charge of combination and conspiracy; and
upon the issue of this trial rests not only the
sanctity of individual freedom, but also the right
of subjects to agitate public questions for trade
purposes or the general weal.
The working men of Canada have started a
"Defence Fund " for the purpose of securing the
best legal talent they can get to defend the repre-
sentatives of their personal rights ; and we appeal
to you for support, inasmuch as your expressions
of sympathy and moral support u ill be the means
of showing the employers of this country that,
though seas divide they do not separate us, cstil,
though locally apart, we are actively allied, and
dust any attempt in one part of the British do-
minions to violate the princi?le of freedom we
have been so long taught to oherish, will only
have the effect of calling forth a scathing rebuke
from all the rest.
The mean and selfish policy pursued by the
employers throughout the whole history of the
agitation, as well as the despicable and
arbitrary measures resorted to to secno
their avowed object, namely, the crushing
of union, is of such a nature that it
cannot fail to call forth manifold expressions of
indignation from a freedom and peace-loving
people; while, on the other hand, the men la)
have been subjected to such abusive ad incon-
siderate usage have conducted themselves in a
way that reflects credit to the cause, and redounds
with honour upon the head of each individual
engaged in the struggle.
We would embrace this opportunity, and press
upon any of our brother tradesmen in the mother
country who contemplate coming to this dominion
the desirability of considering the question in all
its bearings, believing that it would be imprudent
to take such a step while the present dispute is
pending, if, in fact, such a step would not at
any time prove a source of disappointment and
regret.
Any support, whether in the shape of funds or
resolutions supporting our position, will be thank-
fully received and acknowledged in the Ontario
Workman, Toronto Leader, Montreal Star, and
Hamilton Standard, and espies sent to the panel"
pal working men's papers through the
Kingdom.
On behalf of our brethren in Canada, we
remain yours fraternally,
JOHN Hswerr, Toronto Trades Assembly.
THOMAS SHAW, Montreal Nine Hours League.
JAMES Rs-ars, Hamilton Nine Hours League.

articles.title: JULY' 13,, 1872.,
articles.text:
JULY' 13,, 1872.,

THE WEEK'S NEWS.

The Prince and Princess of Wales on
Monday opened the new Home for Con-
valescents at Lauderdale House. There was
an extensive display of bunting in Highgate,
and large numbers of the population turned
out to welcome their Royal Highnesses.

A deputation of working men on Monday
waited upon Mr. Bruce, and presented
memorials pointing out the inoonvemence of
the hours of closing public-houses, as proposed
in the Government Licensing Bill. They
advocated, a uniform dosing at midnight
throughout the country.. Mr. Bruce promised
to lay before his colleagues the representations
made to him, at the same time drawing
attention to the necessity of doing justice
between opposing opinions, and of reaonoiling
the interests of the many with the ineon-
tevienee of the few.

Mr. Walter Spencer Stanhope, of Cannon
Hall, near Barnsley, was on Monday elected,
without- opposition, for the Southern division
of the West Riding, in succession to Lord
Milton. The hon. gentleman was proposed by
Mr. Rowland Winn, M.P. for North Lincoln-
shire, and seconded by Mr. L. R. Starkey, who
was an unsuccessful candidat9 with Mr.
Stanhope for this division at the last general
election.

Captain Burnaby on Monday delivered a
lecture at the Royal United Service Institution
on the education of staff officers in foreign
States. He passed in review the causes which
bad led to the change in the science of war,
and reminded his hearers that much of the
success of the Prussian army was due to what
the officers had learnt in time or peace. If the
autumn mancouvres were properly carried out,
much good must unquestionably result from
them.

Business at Wimbledon commenced on Mon.
day morning, and the shooting was carried on
with considerable spirit. The Alexandra and
the Prince of Wales's Prizes were the principal
competitions of the day. On the following day,
Private Oswald, of the Ist Newcastle, succeeded
in making 20 points for the Queen's Prize at
the 200 yards range. This is the second
occasion within the history of the Association
that such a score has been recorded. ,

At Monday's sitting of the Central Criminal
Court Henry Benson pleaded guilty to having
obtained £l,OOO from Sir Thomas Dakin, late
Mayor of London, by false pretences. He was
sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment.
—Eliza Clift, for the manslaughter of a sales-
man in the New Meat Market, was ordered to
be imprisoned for one month.—James Nicholls,
charged with improper conduct by Major
Charterisi a son of Lord Elcho, was acquitted.
—The indictment against the chairman and
former secretary of the Ottoman Railway
Company was not proceeded with.

Two drunken labourers were on Monday
each sentenced to six months' imprisonment
with hard labour, by Sir Robert Carden for a
violent assault upon a City polioeinan. At
Clerkenwell one sentence of two months, and
two of three weeks each, were passed for
similar offences.

• For a brutal outrage upon a witness a man
named Bentley, was on Monday sentenced to
four months' hard labour by the Bow-street
police magistrate, and ordered, to find A surety
of ato keep the peaoo• for six months. At
the same time a woman who passed as the
prisoner's wife was sent to gaol for two
onths for haying taken part with him in the
assault.

There has been a demonstration of the" Old
Catholic " party at Munich. The Archbishop
of Utreoht, who arrived in the city on Friday
last, held a confirmation in one of the
principal churches on Sunday. An address
was previa voly delivered by Professor
Friedrioh,•tt prominent member of the party,
which was received with enthusiasm. From
liuniat the Archbishop of Utrecht will proceed
to other towns where Old Catholic communi-
ties have been established, and on his return
he will:visit the Palatinate. It is said that
nearly 300 children are to be confirmed by
him.

At a special meeting on Monday the Dublin
Corporation agreed, by a majority of 16 to 4,
to support a petition to Parliament praying
far the removal of Mr. Justice Keogh, By
the precautions taken the life of that judge
would appear to be in some danger, for on
arriving at Kingstown on Monday be was
guarded to the train by a force of police, and
in the next compartment to that which he
oeaupied in travelling by train to Dublin were
number of detectives armed to the teeth.

John IL P. Leighton, one of the sons of the
Rev, Sir Christopher Leighton, Bart,, and a
pupil at Itvpton School, has been killed in the
cricket field by a blow from the ball.

Compliments have passed between the
Republicans of Spain and America on the
occasion of the anniversary of American inde-
pendence. This party has decided on taking
part in the forthcoming elections in Spain.
The Liberal-Conservatives also stand, re-
serving the power of withdrawing under
certain contingencies.

Proof was given at the Boston Jubilee of
the power of music to allay a panic. A cry
of "Fire" having been raised, the bands
struck up the favourite air of "The Star-
spangled Banner," and in their enthnsiasm
the audience forgot their supposed danger and
the excitement was ended. The British band
has sailed on the homeward route, having
achieved an unmistakable success. At the
final concert, the audience rose en masse at the
sound of "God save the Queen."

Oppressive as the heat has been in Europe
during the past week, it has been still more
severely felt in America. The deaths in New
York have, within that period, been more
than three times the average number.

In Saturday's sitting of the French As-
sembly, the Duo de Broglie presented the
report of the Liberation Committee, in which
hopes are expressed that, thanks to the credit
of France, the desired end will soon be con-
summated.• The terms, confessedly hard, are
said to be the best that the Government could
obtain.

It is announced that the Emperor of Ger-
many, previous to deciding on the delicate
San Juan question, has appointed three
law officers of the Crown to report on the
British and American oases.

Notwithstanding previous denials, it is now
stated that the Spanish Treasury has signed
a convention with the Bank of Paris for a
loan of forty millions of francs, on the same
conditions as those of recent financial opera-
tions.

An inquest hold on the body of a French
lady who died suddenly from heart disease in
Rathbone-place, was the moans of calling
forth an expression of opinion on the subject
of coroners' juries. Dr. Potitjohn, of Nov
York and Paris, who Was staying at the
restaurant where the lady died, gave evidenee
that he had been one of the coroners for New
York during twenty years, and that the
coroner's jury was there oomposed of six
gentlemen, a number which was found by ,ex-
perienoe to answer .very well. Dr. Lankester
thought the plan worthy of imitation, though
still holding that, in, serious cases, the coroner
should have power to summon a full jury of
twelve.

An interesting ceremony took plaoe at West
Ham Cemetery on Sunday in the shape of
ereoting a tombstone to the memory of Numa
Hartog, the young Jew who, besides being
Fellow of the University of London, became
Senior Wrangler at Cambridge, and died of
small-pox last year. The tombstone bore an
inscription suitable to the occasion.

Surrey Chapel has secured its new site, and
-religious services were held thereupon on
Sunday, the Rev. Newman Hall stating that
'various creeds had contributed to the sum re-
quired ; the Duchess of Argyll, Lord Similes.
bury, ind the IViarquis of 'Westminster being
among the subscribers. '

Millwall was visited by the Claimant on
Saturday, and the populace vouchsafed him
an enthusiastic reception.

In the Upper HOU% on Monday, Lord
Ripon brought forward the Commons' amend-
ments on the Lords' amendments of the
Ballot Bill. The Government obtained a de-
cisive majority, on the sullied of the optional
ballot, but their lordships insisted on making
the Bill terminable in 1880. Eventually the
Bill passed.

In the House of Commons on Monday, an
animated discussion took place in committee
of supply on the vote to defray the costs of
Governor Eyre's trial, which Was, however,
eventually agreed to •by a majority of 113.

Royal warrants regulating the pay, promo-
tion, and retiring allowances of officers in the
Royal Artillery and Engineers have been
isbued, embodying the suggestions which the
Secretary for War made to Parliament a short.
time since. , In future the captains in both
corps will take the rank of major ; the second
captains will be -made captains; - general
officers and regimental colonels will have a
retiring pension of £6OO a-year ; and the
ordinary and extra rates of pay on aotive
service will be increased all round.

'lt is the intention .of the Duo d'Aumale to
transfer to Chantilly the collection of his
pictures now at Twickenham, which be has
ibrmed during the last twenty years at a cost
of £lOO,OOO, The public is to be admitted
every Sunday to see these works of art' when
they are installed.

The French Government has given up the
idea of taxing raw material, substituting for
it an additional impost upon trade licenses.
The Duo de Chambord has, it is stated,
advised his friends to cease from agitating in
favour of a monarchy, on the ground that
France must be left to select a form of govern-
ment which she thinks best.

Another press duel has taken place in
France. It was fought between M. Tirard,
Deputy for the department of the Seine, and
M. Francis Aubert, an editor of the GankiB.
Both were slightly wound( d.

Turkey, besides those naval and military
preparations to which attention has lately
been drawn, is rapidly developing her railway
system. A telegram from Constantinople
reports the line to Salonica open; and an
livens,' Commission has left for Adrianople
to take in hand the Rou.malian network of
rail ways.

An interesting case for heads of families
came before the Court of Queen's Bench,
raising as it did the important question as to
the liability incurred by removing persons
suffering from infectious diseases, so as to
endanger' the health :of the public. The
plaintiff was a lodging. house. keeper at East-
bourne, and the defendant, a gentleman living
at Holloway. The action was brought to
recover damages for the losses sustained by
the plaintiff through the death of his children
and illness of his wife, and also from his
being prevented from letting his lodgings, in
consequence of the defendant having brought
his family into the house when they were
suffering from scarlet fever, without Stating
the fact. The jury returned a verdict for the
plaintiff, damages ,El2O, with • leave to move
on both sides.

Alice Black, described as being of a hot and
hasty temper; was charged at Clerkenwell with
making a fourth attempt to commit suicide
by cutting her throat. It was explained that
she meant to frighten her lover, and did not
intend to do herself any harm. The chaplain.
reported her as penitent while in the Honse
of Detention, and she was dismissed with a
caution.

Charles Stephen Bore, self-styled 81 reve-
rend," was brought up at Marlborough-street,
charged, at the instance of the Charity Organi-
sation Society, with obtaining money by false
pretences for a so-called National Bible and
Clothing Society.

Two more Communists, Doudouin and
Rouillao, were shot at Satory on Saturday;
the former for murder and arson, the latter
for murder and plunder.

Mr. Justice Keogh has gone on circuit. His
lordship arrived at Longford shortly after 12
o'clock on Tuesday, attended by a numerous
escort of Hussars and constabulary. There
was a large crowd, but no disturbance.

In the action, "Lyon v. Clark," tried in the
Court of Exchequer on Tuesday, the plaintiff,
a lady upwards of 40 years of age, sought to
recover compensation from a licensed victual-
ler of Brighton, for a breach of Promise of
marriage. The defendant pleaded that he had
been exonerated from his undertaking, and
the jury took this view so far as to assess the
damages only at XS.

• The match, open to all comers, for the
Championship at Croquet was commenoed on
Tuesday in the grounds of the All-England
Club, at Wimbledon, The prize offered to
gentlemen was a silver cup, value 50 guineas.
A second prize and the title of Lady Champion
was offered for the competition of ladies. The
play will be continued throughout the week.

Dr. Benjamin Ward . Richardson, M.A.,
F.lt.S., .Honorary Physician to the
Royal Literary Fund, having intimated,
through Lord Houghton, his willingness to
not in the same capacity for the Newspaper
Press Fund, the offer has been most gratefully
accepted by the committee, At the ordinary
monthly meeting of the. committee, on Satur-
day last, the grants made to necessitous mem-
bers and their families exceeded £l6O, in
sums varying from £lO to £m.

The poor widow, Merritt, whose husband
some four mouths ago was shot, whilst pro-
ceeding early ,one morning to his work at the
Lion Brewery, by an Amerioan doctor,in the
Belvedern-rOad, was, on Sunday morning,
delivered of a female child. The mother is
doing as well as can be expected considering
the state of her mind, which has been more or
less defective for some time past.

The ratifications of the new treaty with
Germany were exchanged at Versailles on
Sunday.

The .uyons Exhibition was officially opened
on Monday by the Minister of the Interior,
accompanied by General Bombaki, the Pre-
fect, the local authorities, and. the managing
Committee of the Exhibition.

On Tuesday, the Archbishop of Canter-
bury presided at a meeting held in Lambeth
Palace in connection with the Irish Church
Sustentation Fund. A report was read, show-
ing that the representative body in Ireland
had received £582,077, and that an additional
£37,263 was promised. A resolution was
passed, declaring that the exertions now being
made by the Church in Ireland entitled it to
the sympathy and support of the people of
England, and the meeting pledged itself to
support these efforts.

The sittings 'of the International Prison
Congress were continued on Tuesday, the
Hon. Daniel Haines; of New Jersey, in the
chair. The best mode of giving aid to dis.
charga prisoners, ho w
,to Secure their rehabilita-
tion, the way to repress criminal capitalists,
whether penitentiary systems ought to exclude
all kinds of corporal punishment, and the
treatment of prisoners before conviction, were
amongst the subjects discussed. On Wednesday
the Rev. C. L. Brace, of New York, presided at
the morning sitting, anti Baron Mackay,- one of
the delegates from Holland, at that of the
afternoon.

Attention is drawn by a correspondent to
the importance of the new policy which the
Church is about to adopt in Italy. Hitherto
its motto has been. "Neither Electors nor
Bleated." This is to be superseded by "Vote
and be Victorious." The Pope himself now
urges his partisans to avail themselves of the
legal means at their disposal to make their
opinions prevail. At present the contest is to
be carried on in the municipal eleotions only,
but ere long it is thought that the clergy and
their followers will vote in the. political elec-
tions

. The Journal OJiciel of Tuesday publishes
the text of, the new Convention between
France and Germany, signed at Versailles
on the 29th Jane, and ratified on the 7th
July. Count At nitn, the German. Ambassador
at Versailles, dined with M. Thiers after the
ratification.

Mr. A. Kennard has consented to become,
and has been accepted as, a Conservative
candidate in conjunction With Mr. G. It. Ryder,
at the ensuing election for Salisbury.

--
Prince Arthur, on the invitation of the
Corporation of Leeds, has consented to visit
that town on the 10th of September, on which
day he will open Itoundhay Pa•k, which has
been purchased by the Town Council for a
people's park. The park is 600 acres in extent,
and has been purchased at a cost of £139,000.
It contains a magnificent lake, covering 36
acres.

The offenoe of threatening complainants
and witnesses appears to be on the increase.
There was another case of this kind before
the Clerkenwell police magistrate on Tuesday,
when the defendant, in default of finding
sureties to keep the peace, was sent to prison,

A woman named Margaret Green was on
Tuesday charged at the Southwark Police-
oourt with having caused the death of one
Mary Walsh by striking her on the head.
The fatal occurrence was the result of a
drunken brawl, and as the blow was struck as
far-back as. June 2pd, a remand was granted,
in order that medic:sal evidence might be
forthcoming.

A practice in a well-known restaurant in
St. James's was the cause of a prolonged in-
vestigation at Marlborough-street on Tuesday.
Should a customer divide with a friend any
portion of a dish ordered for himself, an extra
portion is charged for. Two portions of
outlets having been partaken of by three
persons, payment for three was demanded,
and on its being resisted a disturbance arose
which terminated in a charge of assault. The
magistrate expressed his disapproval of the
practice referred to as being neither a legal
nor an equitable one.

A large meting was held at Exeter Hail
on Wednesday in advocacy of the prineiplo of
the Permissive Bill. Sir Thomas Chambers
presided, and Archbishop Manning and Sir
Wilfrid Lawson were amongst the speakers.

A conference,
_under the auspices of the
froward Association, was held on Wednesday,
when resolutions were Passed affirming the
expediency of abolishing capital punishraent.

Mr. Justice ICeogh arrived at Cavan on
Wednesday, escorted by a large force of
military and police. Everything was quiet
on the railway route from Longford, and
Cavan itself.

According to the Poor Law returns, the
number , of paupers in metropolitan work-
houses last week was 31,864 and 72,416
received out-door relief, making a total of
104,280. Compared with the corresponding
week in 1871, 1870, and. 1869, this was a
decrease of 17,397, 23,J16, and 20,888 re-

Mrs. Prodgers having, since her marriage'
fhlierited a sum: of £6,000 through the death
of a relative, arid now being separated from
her husband, has Applied to the Court of
Chincery to settle this sum upon herself and
her children exclusively. Vice-Chancellor
dicided that no ground whatever existed
for dopriviug the husband of [is undoubted
rights under the law, and therefore dismissed
the bill of Mrs. Prodgers with oasts.

At Marlborough-street Polio Court, Henry
Taylor, .described as a sham Doctor of Phi-
losophy,. was sentenced to a lengthened term
of inaprisonmeut for having defrauded Mr.
.Tuliari Golds-mid, M.P. and others. .4t the
Same court, Mary Preston was sentenced to
three •montla hard. labour for having ob.
tained money by fraud from the Earl of Dun-
more.

• A fearful crime was perpetrated in Hoxton
on Wednesday. ' Shortly after one o'clock in
the day it was discovered that a widow
named Squires, and her daughter, who carried
on the business of stationers at 41, Hyde-
road, in that neighbourhood, had been
barbarously murdered. The tragedy had 'ap-
parently been committed about an hour pre-
viously, but no alarm had been given. From
the fact that the house was ransacked from
top to bottom, it is supposed that plunder was
the primary cause of the crime.

Mr. Horace Greeley has been nominated for
the Presidency of the United States by the
Democratic, Convention at Baltimore. Six
'hundred and eighty-six yntea were given in
his favour, and. thirty-eight againbt him.
The Convention has adopted the Cincinnati
" platform."

• The adjournedfirst meeting under the bank •
ruptey of -the claimn.nt to the Tichborne
baronetcy has been still further pokponed for
oix .months, in • consequence of the pro-
ceedings now pending against the bankrupt.

fatal- occurrence was the result of a quarrel in

Monday. The prisoner was sentenced to,five

beries from offices in Gray's-inn. tfpen one of

The half-year's dividend to the shareholders
In the Brighton-line will be los. per cent on
